en: The Dhāraṇī Sūtra on the Innumerable Gateways Entering All Dharmas as Asked by the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā,
translated by the Northern Qi layman Wan Tianyi.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
There were twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
all of whom were in their final birth before attaining buddhahood,
who had gathered there from other worlds.
They have attained dhāraṇīs and possess inexhaustible eloquence;
they have accomplished mindfulness and wisdom, are endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame,
and encounter no obstacles regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas.
They act as uninvited friends to all sentient beings,
drawing near to teach and transform them so that they may accomplish wholesome dharmas;
they travel to and fro among all Buddha-fields without obstruction.
According to the minds of sentient beings, they teach and transform them through various wholesome dharmas.
They remain free from all realms of demonic activity and eliminate all enemies that are the afflictions.
They are skillfully able to universally enter all dharma-realms;
they are skillfully able to make offerings to all Buddhas;
and they are skillfully able to dwell securely in all meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis.
Furthermore, they were able to enter and emerge at will with sovereign mastery.
Their names were the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amṛtadundubhi and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amṛtaghoṣa.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amṛtaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amṛtanāman,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amṛtaghoṣa.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śālarāja,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvamanojñaghoṣa,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvajñatālakṣaṇa.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Saṃkhyālakṣaṇa,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Amṛtapraveśa,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantamati.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantābhyudgata,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantanāman.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantanimitta,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantarāja,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaguṇanimittavaiśvārājendra.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subtle Sound,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Supreme Mark,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Invincible.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Eye;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Virtue of Universal Vision;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Manifesting No Fault or Evil.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is free from faults;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is without transgressions or evils;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is a friend to all sentient beings without being asked.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who does not abandon any sentient beings;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who always delights in accumulating all merits;
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the Excellent Vehicle.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Renowned for Supreme Merit,
and twelve thousand other such leading Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
together with eighty thousand devaputras headed by Yama-devaputra.
There were eight billion devaputras of Tuṣita Heaven;
nine thousand two hundred nayutas of devaputras of Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and fifteen thousand nayutas of devaputras of Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.
All the gods from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations up to the immeasurable heavens of the Form Realm all came to assemble.
At that time, to the east, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ninety-two Buddha-worlds...
There is a world named Invincible.
In it dwells a Buddha named Tathāgata Well-Arisen Power.
Therein is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Honorable Victory.
Surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas before and behind him,
he vanished from that world-system in a single thought-moment and suddenly appeared in this Sahā world.
Abiding in the midst of space,
each of those bodhisattvas emitted clouds of lapis lazuli that completely covered the trichiliocosm.
It rained flowers of Jambūnada gold.
Each bodhisattva individually rained down as many articles of offering as there are atoms in a buddha-world.
Each bodhisattva individually rained down immeasurable varieties of flowers, produced on both water and land, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-world.
Each and every bodhisattva rained down as many subtle and variegated incenses as there are atoms in a single buddha-world.
Each and every bodhisattva also rained down clouds of sandalwood, aloeswood, black hard aloeswood, and various mixed incenses, numbering as many as the atoms in a single buddha-world.
Each bodhisattva rained down as many garlands of the seven treasures as there are atoms in a buddha-world;
each bodhisattva rained down as much sandalwood incense as there are atoms in a buddha-world.
Each and every bodhisattva rained down various kinds of exquisite celestial and human garments, as numerous as the atoms in a single buddha-world;
each and every bodhisattva rained down various kinds of banners and streamers adorned with diverse jewels, as numerous as the atoms in a single buddha-world.
Each and every bodhisattva uttered verses equal in number to the atoms within a buddha-world to offer praise;
these were all unprecedented eulogies of the Tathāgata.
At that time, in this Sahā world...
All sentient beings suffering in the hells shall attain peace and happiness;
all sentient beings shall regard one another with a mind of loving-kindness;
and all hungry ghosts shall be completely satiated.
All sentient beings were free from greed, hatred, and delusion;
they were neither cold nor hot, devoid of conceptual desires, and neither hungry nor thirsty.
The days were clear and mild, without dust or mist.
At that time, all sentient beings were free from any lack of satisfaction regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and they abandoned their heedlessness;
all the devas attained tranquility.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Saṃkusumitarāja ascended as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Abiding in mid-air, they rained down various articles of offering to make offerings to the Tathāgata:
all kinds of flower garlands, mixed incenses, ointments, powdered incenses, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and various precious, wondrous ornaments.
It rained upon all the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the abodes of the yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
They filled the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and extended throughout the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Saṃkusumitarājendra descended from above and approached the presence of the World-Honored One.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and circumambulated him countless times.
He then covered the Tathāgata with a celestial, pure net of lapis lazuli and diamond beads and sat to one side.
At that time, the Honored and Victorious One saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, enter the Dharma of the Single True Reality.
Upon entering this Dharma,
he was able to enter all the Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
He is able to know the Buddhas' immeasurable eloquence of correspondence,
eloquence of liberation,
and unimpeded eloquence.
Unattached eloquence;
inexhaustible eloquence;
eloquence in all circumstances.
The eloquence of universal discernment;
the eloquence of teaching all dharmas through skillful means according to reality;
and the eloquence of the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The eloquence that clearly explains all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis through skillful means as they truly are;
the eloquence that explains right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*) and the arising and ceasing [of phenomena];
and the eloquence that explains the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and their progression.
The eloquence of the faculties, powers, and knowledge;
the invincible eloquence of the powers;
and the eloquence that awakens to reality as it truly is.
The analytical discernment of the dharma-realm;
the discernment that perceives reality as it is;
and the discernment that all phenomena are like illusions, transformations, bubbles, mirages, the moon reflected in water, and echoes.
He correctly discerns that which is neither arising nor ceasing;
he discerns the subtle;
he discerns the manifold.
He possesses exquisite eloquence;
he knows the minds of sentient beings as they truly are, whether virtuous or non-virtuous,
and he possesses the power of eloquence to speak with a single voice amidst all assemblies.
At that time, when the Sarvadharmapratibhāna saw such a sight,
he rose from his seat and adjusted his robes.
Placing his right knee on the ground and joining his palms toward the Buddha,
he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I pray that you grant me a brief moment of leisure."
"Listen as I question the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇottama:
"I constantly bestow upon sentient beings the gift of solitude."
"Ask whatever you wish;
the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, shall sever your doubts and gladden your mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃpūjita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān,
there is a dhāraṇī called 'The Dharma-gate of the Teaching of All Dharmas as They Are, Immeasurable.
If there is a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī and its corresponding dharma-gate,"
That bodhisattva is able to attain uninterrupted eloquence,
unerring eloquence,
and the eloquence that renders all phenomena as neither created nor uncreated.
They possess knowledge of dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence,
as well as subtle discernment,
enabling them to uphold all that has been spoken by all Buddhas.
They are able to know the immeasurable teachings spoken [by the Buddhas],
and further, they are able to enter the wisdom of the collection of dhāraṇīs,
the wisdom of the elements (dhātu), and the wisdom of the faculties (indriya).
Entering the wisdom of ultimate truth;
entering the wisdom of all sentient beings;
entering the wisdom of non-sentient beings.
Entering into the cognition of existence;
entering into the cognition of non-existence;
entering into the cognition of attachment.
Entering the wisdom of non-attachment;
entering the wisdom of emptiness;
entering the wisdom of non-emptiness.
Entering the knowledge of having conceptualization; entering the knowledge of being without conceptualization;
entering the knowledge of having aspiration.
He enters the knowledge of wishlessness;
he enters the knowledge that has a basis;
he enters the knowledge that is without basis.
The wisdom that enters into the conditioned;
the wisdom that enters into the unconditioned;
and the wisdom that enters into a single point and attains unhindered eloquence.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One,
out of compassion for all beings, will expound this gateway of dhāraṇīs.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Uṣṇīṣavijayā, saying:
Excellent, excellent,
O Exalted One!
It is well that you are able to ask the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, about this matter.
"O Uṣṇīṣavijayā,
listen attentively now and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you."
At that time, Jinaśrī received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha said to Jinaśrī,
"What is the *Sarvadharmanirdeśānantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*?"
At that time, the World-Honored One then spoke it:
*Śrī-tattvam-anantāya-śri*.

The Emperor descended into the Samantakusumasaṃstāraka-buddhānujñāta-vyūha; such is the supreme and majestic.
This is the dhāraṇī of the entrance into immeasurable gateways of all dharmas.
If a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī,
they will be able to uphold everything spoken by all buddhas.
They are able to travel through all the worlds of the Buddhas;
they are able to retain everything spoken by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
and they are able to retain all worldly scriptures, medical treatises, incantations, and Vedic texts.
He is able to produce and enter into the speech of all sentient beings;
he knows the minds of all sentient beings and is skilled in all languages, words, and sounds.
According to their speech and sounds, they are able to reach all such paths;
they are able to know the true and the untrue dharmas, attain firm mindfulness,
and become worthy of the offerings of all bodhisattvas.
One is able to move all Buddha-worlds with a single finger,
yet cause those sentient beings to have no thought of alarm or fear;
one is able to know the three periods of time in a single thought-moment.
It can sever all doubts and regrets of sentient beings;
it can cause sentient beings to cultivate resolute practice without further hesitation or obstruction;
and they shall constantly attain wholesome mindfulness, never again relying on various devas.
They attain immeasurable gateways of samādhi and obtain the knowledge of past lives;
they always undergo miraculous birth and never receive birth from a womb.
One who sits upon a lotus flower will never again be born in the evil realms;
wherever they take up a body,
that body shall be free from all openings for parasites.
In all places of birth, they shall always obtain this dhāraṇī;
they shall never be born in a land where no Buddha resides;
and they shall always possess an inexhaustible treasure-hand.
They attain the adornment of Buddha-fields;
they attain skillful means as they truly are to teach and transform sentient beings;
and they are able to know all the conduct of sentient beings.
They are able to know the wholesome and unwholesome minds of sentient beings;
they are able to know all the dharmas practiced by non-Buddhists;
they have attained the skillful means of eloquent exposition and the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury.
They attain the Sudhīra dhāraṇī;
they attain the Pauṣmika dhāraṇī;
they attain the Amitavyūha dhāraṇī.
One attains the dhāraṇī of retaining all that is heard and the dhāraṇī of fearlessness.
Furthermore, it is most supreme.
To state the essentials:
this person is able to attain the *dhāraṇī* of non-forgetfulness equal in number to the atoms within the space of all Buddha-fields and the dharma-realm;
and they attain [the *dhāraṇī*] equal in number to the drops of water in all worlds within the dharma-realm and the realm of space.
They attain such dhāraṇīs of non-forgetfulness as these;
they attain the dharma-realm and the space-realm throughout all buddha-fields until the end of the future.
Within that space, there is a great fire,
and one attains such *dhāraṇīs* of non-forgetfulness as those that perceive the equal number of births and cessations of all its flames.
Furthermore, having attained such a dharma-realm and space-realm,
one takes all Buddha-fields and the great earth with its grasses and trees throughout the limits of the future,
and grinds them into atoms of dust.
They attain such a dhāraṇī of non-forgetfulness regarding these numbers.
Furthermore, they attain [the realization of] all Buddha-fields throughout the dharma-realm and the space-realm,
reaching to the end of the future.
By means of the dhāraṇī of non-forgetfulness as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and as minute as motes of dust,
one attains such dhāraṇīs as the "dhāraṇī of the present mindfulness of all Buddhas" and others;
thus it is most supreme.
A bodhisattva who has attained such a dhāraṇī is able to attain hundreds of thousands of such inconceivable dhāraṇīs,
and even inconceivable, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi.
It is most supreme.
If there is anyone who skillfully recites this and keeps it in mind,
that person will have no fear of non-humans, no fear of rākṣasas, and no fear of piśācas.
If one stays in an araṇya (forest hermitage),

there will be no fear of piśācas, nor fear of lions, tigers, wolves, other predatory beasts, venomous insects, thieves, bandits, or wicked people, nor any such fears as those that cause the hair to stand on end.
If one recites this dhāraṇī,
even if seized by any malevolent spirits or ghosts, one will swiftly obtain liberation.
If one recites this dhāraṇī...
All poisons, whether within the body or outside the body, shall be unable to cause harm.
Wherever this dhāraṇī is recited, [no calamity shall arise].
Whether in a village or a town,
whether among a multitude or in a monastic dwelling,
or at a place for walking meditation.
Ultimately, there will be no fear of any resuscitating spirits,
such as those raised through various methods, nor of kings, bandits, water, fire, blades, poisons, evil ghosts, humans, non-humans, or venomous dragons.
Furthermore, O Honored One,
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—
whether they be householders or those who have gone forth—
Practicing pure conduct and wearing pure garments,
one should offer fine incense and flowers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
while keeping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind.
Recite this dhāraṇī.

If there is a sick person—whether suffering from a headache, malaria, wind disorders, fever, or cold disorders; or if sentient beings suffer from convulsions lasting one day, two days, three days, or four days.
Whether it be chronic illness, eye pain, toothache, abdominal pain, or back pain;
or malignant winds, loss of mindfulness, or possession by spirits—
such diseases as these.
If this person recites this dhāraṇī and rubs it with their hand,
it will become most excellent.
If one recites this dhāraṇī one hundred and ninety-eight times,
it is impossible that any illnesses or fears would not be eliminated.
For what reason?
Because the Buddhas of the past protected sentient beings by means of this dhāraṇī.
The Buddhas of the future will also protect sentient beings with this dhāraṇī,
as will the Buddhas of the present.
Furthermore, Venerable One, this dhāraṇī also protects and sustains sentient beings.
This dhāraṇī is most supreme.
Possessing great merit and great power,
they bring vast benefit to sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings...
For those who skillfully recite this dhāraṇī and maintain it in their hearts,
eight billion yakṣas will protect them.
At that time, within the assembly...
There was a yakṣa king named Śarabha who,
together with a thousand attendants,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
we, together with our retinues,
shall always provide protection for those who recite this dhāraṇī.
World-Honored One,
within the Great Snow Mountains there is an excellent medicinal herb named "Benefiting Vital Essence."
By the power of this medicine's virtue,
it can cause all medicinal herbs throughout Jambudvīpa to increase in their potency,
World-Honored One.
I shall constantly sprinkle this wondrous medicine upon this person to augment their vital strength.
May those who recite this dhāraṇī never suffer the pain of illness;
may their bodies and minds be peaceful and secure, free from any ailment, and may they have no evil dreams while lying down to sleep.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Bhadrajyotis:
"Until those Four Great Heavenly Kings attain Buddhahood,"
They shall always protect those who recite this dhāraṇī and never abandon them,
even unto the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The devaputras of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati,
and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens shall constantly protect this person until they attain Buddhahood.
Most Exalted One!
Those who uphold this dhāraṇī shall not perceive the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
If one does not apprehend the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
then one does not apprehend any phenomena whatsoever.
One who does not apprehend any phenomena will swiftly accomplish this dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, O Venerable One,
all phenomena are truly unattainable;
it is only by means of conventional linguistic designations that they are called aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Because of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, they are called "accumulations.
Yet, in reality, all dharmas have no accumulation. Why is this?
Because the nature of form cannot be apprehended,
it is as when earth is established by its own nature, water by its own nature, fire by its own nature, and wind by its own nature.
Thus, these great elements are accomplished by their own nature;
they neither increase nor decrease, nor do they aggregate.
They are truly unobtainable and have no location.
How is it that name-and-form are like form?
Earth, water, fire, and wind are likewise so.
In the past, there was no agent.
In the future there is no agent;
in the present there is no agent. Why is this?
All phenomena are formless,
colorless, without birth, and without cessation.
If a phenomenon is not born, it does not cease.
If there is no arising and ceasing, then there is no activity.
Furthermore, it is said that because form exists, there are the past, future, and present;
yet this form is truly unattainable.
If form is truly unapprehendable,
one should know that there is no past, future, or present. For this reason,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Therefore, one who is able to enter is precisely one who enters the dhāraṇī.
One who enters this dhāraṇī is said to have entered these aggregates (skandhas).
If one enters these aggregates, it is called attaining the dhāraṇī.
This dhāraṇī is called "holding.
What is it that this holding holds?
To maintain that which is non-apprehensible is what is called "maintaining.
As for what is termed "apprehension":
Because of the nature of linguistic conventions,
there is a provisional conjunction of names and sounds;
in reality, nothing is attained, yet it is provisionally designated as "action."
In reality, there are no aggregates and no sense bases;
in reality, there is no dharma that can be grasped. Why is this?
This unconditioned phenomenon is conventionally designated as "form.
How could this unconditioned phenomenon be accumulated?
If something can be accumulated, it is conventionally designated as an "aggregate" (skandha).
If they were not accumulated, how could they be called "aggregates" (skandha)?
Furthermore, Venerable One,
it is because many dharmas are gathered together.
It is called a "house" and it is called a "city. For example,
when there is ground, walls, beams, pillars, rafters, eaves, doors, gates, and windows, it is called a house.
Because it is a collection of many houses, lanes, streets, towers, gatehouses, battlements, defensive walls, gardens, groves, ponds,
and moats, it is called a "city.
If one were separated from these various things, a city could not be found.
"So it is, so it is, O Venerable One.
It is through the provisional conjunction of various conditions."
This is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
When one seeks its true nature, it is truly unobtainable.
If it is unobtainable, how can there be any accumulation?
If there were no aggregation, where would form exist?
As it is with form, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, O Venerable One:
If one enters these aggregates, it is called entering the gateway of the dhāraṇī.
Most Exalted One,
this dhāraṇī is also unapprehendable.
Why is this? Just as the eye cannot be apprehended and the realm of the eye cannot be apprehended,
so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Why is this? Because herein nothing real can be apprehended.
That which cannot be apprehended as real is called "non-entity."
If there were no entities, there would be no accomplishment;
if there were no accomplishment, there would be no arising;
and if there were no arising, there would be no cessation.
If there were no arising and ceasing, there would be no past, future, or present.
It is only because of worldly phenomena that names and speech exist;
yet these names and speech have no real existence whatsoever.
Sentient beings likewise have no speech;
worldly phenomena likewise have no attachment.
That which is without attachment is precisely that which has no speech.
These phenomena are truly unattainable;
they truly have no substance.
If there is truly no substance, there is also no accomplishment.
If there is no accomplishment, there is no arising;
if there is no arising, there is no cessation;
and if there is neither arising nor cessation, there are no three periods of time.
If the three periods of time do not exist, then there are no names;
if there are no names, then there are no characteristics;
if there are no characteristics, then there is no verbal expression.
There is no accumulation and no attachment;
there is no going and no coming, no realization and no attainment;
it is not the stage of ordinary beings.
It is not the stage of the śrāvaka;
it is not the stage of the pratyekabuddha;
it is not the stage of the bodhisattva.
Nor is it the stage of a Buddha.
It is neither a stage nor not a stage.
If it is neither a stage nor not a stage, [then...]
It is called "suchness" (tathatā),
yet it is neither suchness nor non-suchness;
it is quiescent and signless.
Furthermore, it is by means of conventional linguistic dharmas that one is designated as a Tathāgata. Why is this?
By virtue of the ultimate truth,
this ultimate truth is non-existent;
it is truly unattainable.
That which is thus unapprehendable is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Venerable One,
it is like the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element, up to and including the eighteen elements.
For the sake of linguistic convention,
a name is assigned to it,
such as "the earth element."
For the sake of communicating the Dharma to sentient beings,
one establishes various names in such and such ways.
Venerable One,
this linguistic dharma is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
To enter this Dharma-realm is called entering this *dhāraṇī*.
In that context, as for what is called "entering," what is meant by "entering"?
That which is called "entering" is entering into that which is not entered. Why is this?
All dharmas are in reality devoid of any substantial entity.
If they are in reality devoid of substance, then there is no accomplishment.
If there is no accomplishment, then there is no arising.
If there is no arising, then there is no cessation.
If there is neither arising nor cessation, then there are no three periods of time.
It is only for the sake of all phenomena that names and designations are provisionally established.
However, these phenomena, as well as their verbal designations and names,
are in reality empty and signless dharmas;
if they are signless, they are likewise wishless.
If it is wishless, then there is no coming or going,
no movement, and no conceptual proliferation. Good son!
The true nature of all phenomena is thus:
it is without deception and is most sublime.
In future ages, if there are good men or good women who write down, read,
recite, or explain this dhāraṇī to others;
Regarding the merit obtained by this person,
there is none except the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is able to describe it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished preaching this sutra, [entered parinirvāṇa].
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
all the devas performed various musical performances and rained down celestial flowers.
Eighty-four thousand people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
one thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path;
and nine thousand three hundred devas likewise resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, the Honored Victorious One (Guruśrī), all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had gathered from other directions,
the Yakṣa King Jambhaka,
and the entire great assembly of devas, humans, and others.
The gandharvas, asuras, and others,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At that time, the kings of the gods of the three thousand suns and moons, and the dragon kings, [gathered]. *The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of the Immeasurable Dhāraṇī Entering All Phenomena as Asked by the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā*.
The various asura kings,
the lords of the great spirits of heaven and earth, the celestial Māra kings, the fire-king deities,
the mountain-king deities, the tree-king deities, and all other such king deities.
Immediately before the Buddha, he joined his palms in salutation and said:
"To those who practice and recite this mantra,
I shall go daily to make offerings."
One will not die an untimely death,
and all evils shall find no opportunity.
Wherever this dhāraṇī is maintained, [it shall prevail].
The various heavenly kings, the various asura kings, and the great ghost generals all together respectfully protect and serve him.
One who studies this mantra will personally attain Buddhahood. (From "At that time" onwards, five pages are missing from the Danzang.)
Ācārya, mahā-ācārya, jaraṇī, ukkamu-kha, sapati, mahā-sapati; one should receive, uphold, recite, and chant these mantra phrases.
One who knows their births over seven lifetimes and upholds [this teaching] shall not be harassed or approached by any bhūtas, spirits, humans, or non-humans.
Vicious snakes dare not sting;
poisonous drugs are naturally eliminated;
even blades cannot cause injury.
The king did not dare to harm him,
and Brahmā likewise felt no anger toward him.
This was spoken by seventy billion Buddhas.
Whoever violates this mantra shall incur a grave offense.
Furthermore, there are eighty bodhisattvas, including Maitreya and others;
I too shall now proclaim this dhāraṇī of sustaining phrases.
Ajñājñā | Ṭakhaṭara | Rarili-mi | Dvāru-mi | Śali | Tiri-śu. Recite, chant, and read these dhāraṇī phrases.
One knows the past lives of fourteen kalpas.
This dhāraṇī-mantra was spoken by eighty-four billion Buddhas;
whoever violates this mantra shall incur grave retribution.
Ajivajī, naji-kujana, jiti-ri, śarāvatī-anavatī, panatī, kāhani, mahākāhani—receive, uphold, maintain, recite, chant, and read these mantra-words.
One who knows their own past lives through countless eons and upholds this [sūtra] shall not be dared to harass or approach by any *bhūta* spirits, ghosts, or non-human beings.
Vicious serpents dare not sting;
poisonous drugs are naturally eliminated;
even blades cannot cause injury.
The king also did not dare to harm him,
and Brahmā likewise felt no anger toward him.
This dhāraṇī-mantra was spoken by countless billions of Buddhas.
Whoever violates this mantra shall incur grave retribution.
This is the dhāraṇī of the Holding-Phrase;
by means of this mantra, one can cause even a withered tree to sprout flowers and leaves.
May a hundred ailments be eliminated and one naturally attain peace and security;
may all harm and calamity be warded off.
*Namo Buddha*, may all my incantations fulfill their aspirations.
The Buddha Spoke the Dhāraṇī-pātra.

I now likewise expound this for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings:
if anyone hears this mantra, they will give rise to vast faith and joy,
and be able to remember their past lives, even up to fourteen births.
If a person possesses a mind of faith and joy, and hears and upholds this mantra,
then wherever they dwell or come from, they shall not encounter any calamities or hardships,
nor shall they be harmed by humans, non-humans, kumbhāṇḍas, or pūtanas.
Though they may cause affliction and distress, by reciting and upholding this mantra,
one will not be wounded by blades, nor can poison harm them,
nor shall they be killed by others, because of reciting and upholding this mantra.
The celestial Māra Pāpīyān, though most honored within the realm of desire,
cannot create obstacles for one who recites and upholds this mantra;
likewise, parents, brothers, kinsmen, and friends [shall not cause harm].
One shall not encounter various misfortunes or calamities because of reciting and upholding this mantra;
even unwholesome karma created over hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas can be purified in seven days by reciting and upholding this mantra.
The various merits accumulated by a Bodhisattva over a hundred million eons can be surpassed in seven days by one who recites and maintains this mantra; thus,
the Four Great Heavenly Kings and others shall protect the four directions of the world.
Kubera, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūpākṣa, and Virūḍhaka,
along with their ministers and retinues, shall joyfully praise,
revere, and constantly protect [the practitioner] because they recite and uphold this mantra.
The Tathāgata King Fully Endowed with Peaceful Security entrusts this to you: may you swiftly attain the unsurpassed path, just as the Tathāgata King Fully Endowed with Dark Beryl did;
may all evil deeds committed over billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas be utterly eliminated, and may you quickly attain clear understanding of the teaching.
Flying to all lands, may one swiftly attain the path of Nirvāṇa.

During the era of the Northern Qi dynasty,
there was a lay practitioner named Wan Tianyi,
whose original surname was Tuoba (pronounced Tuo-ba).
Bei Dai was a native of Yúnzhōng.
During the division of surnames by the Wèi dynasty,
he took the surname Wàn (pronounced "mùqí").
His family had resided in Luoyang for generations;
thus, he was again considered a native of Henan. It was an error to title him "Indic" (Tianzhu);
later, he was simply referred to as the Wan clan.
In his youth, Yi had once left the household life and studied under a Brahmin;
he was intelligent and possessed great resolve and vigor.
He was proficient in both Brahmi script and the Sanskrit language, and was also skilled in incantations and esoteric arts;
consequently, when summoned, he was permitted to participate in the work of translation and transmission.
In the Zhanying year of Emperor Wucheng’s reign,
he personally translated at the capital of Ye one fascicle of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*,
which was widely circulated throughout the world; it shares the same root text as the *Anantapāramitā-dhāraṇī*.
